The agents are connected by an undirected communication graph encoded by a symmetric, doubly stochastic mixing matrixW∈R N×N , and they can exchange messages only with their neighbors according toW. In this setting, decentralized optimization already offers several correction mechanisms for heterogeneity, including gradient tracking, EXTRA, and ED/D 2 [8, 13, 15]. SUDA is particularly appealing because it expresses many of these schemes inside one primal–dual recursion parameterized by three matrices(A,B,C)built fromW[2]. On the optimizer side, Muon replaces a coordinatewise step by a matrix polarization direction and has shown strong empirical performance in centralized and federated settings [7, 9, 10, 14]. What is still missing is a framework that lets these two viewpoints meet cleanly: we would like to vary the communication backbone without redesigning the Muon update from scratch every time. Current decentralized Muon results do not yet provide that picture. DeMuon [6] combines Muon with gradient tracking and works over general graphs, but it is built around one specific communication template. This leaves four questions open. Can Muon be placed inside a unified SUDA-style backbone? Can one obtain a topology-separated rate in the nuclear-norm geometry induced by Muon, rather than an analysis in which network effects and optimizer geometry are entangled from the start? Is tracking before polarization genuinely necessary, or merely convenient? And, compared with server-

based/federated Muon, can a fully decentralized Muon update still exploit the usual linear-speedup effect from averaging stochastic gradients? We answer these questions with SUDA–Muon, which keeps Muon’s matrix geometry but places it inside the SUDA primal–dual recursion. The point is not only to obtain one more decentralized Muon method. It is to expose which parts of the behavior come from the communication mechanism and which parts come from the polarization step itself. Our contributions are the following.

blocks.text: Matrix-Aware Optimizers and the Muon Family in Centralized Training
heading_path: Matrix-Aware Optimizers and the Muon Family in Centralized Training

blocks.text: Muon was introduced as an optimizer that acts directly on matrix-valued parameters through a polarization step instead of treating every layer as a flattened vector [7]. Subsequent empirical work reports strong performance on modern architectures, including large language models, and recent theory interprets Muon as steepest descent under a spectral-norm constraint [9, 12, 16]. For our purposes, the important point is not merely that Muon is matrix-aware, but that its update rule is nonlinear at the matrix level. That nonlinearity is exactly what complicates decentralization. A broader literature studies structured optimizers such as Adafactor and Shampoo [5, 11]. These methods also exploit matrix or tensor structure, but they do not raise the same question considered here. Our focus is narrower: how to combine Muon’s polarization step with fully decentralized correction mechanisms over sparse graphs.

blocks.text: Decentralized SGD is simple but biased under heterogeneous data. EXTRA, Exact Diffusion/D2, and gradient tracking were developed to remove or reduce that bias through additional correction terms [13, 15, 17]. SUDA is especially relevant because it places several of these methods inside one primal–dual template parameterized by (A,B,C), making it possible to compare communication mechanisms without redesigning the algorithm each time [1, 18]. Most of this literature, however, works in a Euclidean setting: gradients are communicated linearly, and the optimizer itself is vector-based or at most diagonally preconditioned. The resulting theory says a great deal about topology and bias correction, but it does not address what happens when the optimizer applies a nonlinear matrix transformation before the update.

blocks.text: Distributed Muon: Decentralized and Federated Extensions
heading_path: ReasFlow Paper Copilot / CSIAM Trans. Appl. Math.,x(20xx), pp. 1-50
Distributed Muon: Decentralized and Federated Extensions

blocks.text: Distributed extensions of Muon are already beginning to appear. Federated variants such as FedMuon study star-topology settings and show that naive local Muon combined with FedAvg can be unstable under heterogeneity, which motivates additional server-side correction [10, 14]. Those works are informative about heterogeneity, but they do not address fully decentralized communication. DeMuon is, to our knowledge, the clearest fully decentralized Muon method on general graphs [6]. It demonstrates that combining Muon with gradient tracking is viable, but it is organized around one specific communication template. Our paper differs in emphasis: we ask for a unified SUDA-style backbone for Muon, a topology-separated rate within that backbone, a direct statement that tracking before polarization is not merely helpful but necessary in general, and an explicit counterexample separating the linearspeedup behavior of federated and fully decentralized Muon.

With the master bound established, we now draw two structural consequences. We first instantiate it for concrete SUDA communication backbones in Subsection 4.4 and then show in Subsection 4.5 that tracking before polarization is not a modular detail but a structural requirement. Section 5 then turns to a complementary counterexample on federated versus fully decentralized linear speedup.

The difference lies in constants rather than order. ED/D2 and EXTRA use 1−γ= (1− λ)(1+λ), whereas ATC-GT uses 1−γ=1−λ. Whenλis close to one, ATC-GT therefore carries a larger prefactor in the subdominant network terms, even though the asymptotic order is the same. This is precisely the modularity provided by the SUDA formulation: among convergent SUDA instantiations, the leading stochastic term is graph-free, and the communication backbone changes only the transient network corrections through the substitution forγ. In short, the theory does not predict different dominant rates for ED/D 2, EXTRA, and ATC-GT. It predicts the same leading order and different transient behavior. This modularity, however, has a clear limit: changing the backbone within SUDA affects only transient terms, but changing the order between tracking and polarization does not. The next subsection shows that moving tracking after polarization can destroy convergence altogether.

We now turn to a different design choice that is not modular in this sense: whether Muon polarizes a tracked quantity or a purely local one. The following proposition shows that if we remove this pre-polarization tracking step while keeping the rest of the algorithm unchanged, then one cannot, in general, guaranteeexactconvergence to stationarity for heterogeneous objectives. blocks.text: We use two benchmarks that stress different parts of the decentralized Muon story: CIFAR-100 with strong cross-node heterogeneity, and GPT-2 fine-tuning on Wikitext-2 with a much milder, near-IID partition. Throughout, we compare SUDA–MUON-ED, SUDA–MUON-ATC-GT, and DEMUON, and all quantitative summaries are computed from pre-aggregated CSV logs produced by the training scripts. For CIFAR-100, we use the standard 50,000/10,000 train/test split, a ResNet-18-style model with 100 output classes, and a Dirichlet partition with concentrationα=0.05, which produces severe label skew across workers. The main comparison usesN=10 nodes on a ring with mixing parameterρ=0.25, batch size 512 per node, constant stepsizeη=0.03, EMA parameterβ=0.9, weight decay 5×10 −4, and 25 training epochs. Unless otherwise stated, each configuration is run with 3 random seeds, and we report the performance of the averaged model. We also include two CIFAR-100 extensions aimed at the communication story. First, fixing SUDA–MUON-ED, we vary the topology and node count overN∈{4,8,12}to isolate how system scale changes the preferred graph. Second, we run a larger and longer experiment withN=20 ring-connected nodes for 100 epochs using a slightly smaller constant stepsizeη=0.01. This long-horizon setting is where steady-state communication effects should be easiest to see. For GPT-2/Wikitext-2, each node hosts the pretrainedgpt2model. We tokenize the corpus into length-512 sequences, use local batch size 16, train for 4 epochs with base

stepsizeη=0.03, and apply a warmup-plus-cosine schedule. The main comparison uses a 15-node ring, while the ablation again varies topology and node count for SUDA– MUON-ED. Each GPT configuration is run with 2 seeds, and we report validation perplexity at epoch 4.

blocks.text: This paper studies one specific obstruction in fully decentralized Muon: the polarization step is nonlinear, so it does not interact with gossip averaging in the same way as an ordinary gradient step. SUDA–Muon addresses that obstruction by placing Muon inside the SUDA primal–dual backbone, which lets us compare several decentralized correction mechanisms within one template. The main theoretical message is that the dominant stochastic term remains topologyfree, while the graph enters only through faster-decaying corrections. The main structural message is even simpler: tracking before polarization is not optional in general. Without it, one can construct smooth heterogeneous problems on which the averaged iterate stays at a non-stationary point. The second conceptual message is a contrast with federated Muon. In our linearspeedup counterexample, server-side averaging before polarization recovers the usual σ/ √ Nvariance reduction, while fully decentralized local polarization before averaging does not, even on a complete graph with exact averaging. Our experiments on CIFAR-100 and GPT-2/Wikitext-2 are consistent with this picture. Short-horizon and near-IID runs make the decentralized Muon variants look simi-

lar, but in the 20-node, 100-epoch non-IID CIFAR-100 setting both SUDA-based variants outperform DEMUON, with SUDA–MUON-ED performing best. When the partition is near IID, the different SUDA–Muon instances behave much more similarly and the best topology can shift. Natural next steps include communication-efficient variants with compression, sharper rates under additional structure such as PL-type conditions, online tuning of the stepsize and EMA parameters, and larger-scale experiments that test whether the same topology effects persist for bigger models and graphs.

blocks.text: Abstract.Decentralized stochastic optimization is a standard framework for largescale learning over networks where a central coordinator is unavailable or undesirable. In this paper we proposeMulti-Gossip Accelerated DSGD(MC-ADSGD), a decentralized stochastic optimization algorithm that combines a Nesterov-type primal–dual extrapolation with a multi-round accelerated gossip averaging primitive (FGA). At each outer iteration, the proposed algorithm performs two calls to FGA with gossip depth R, thereby allowing multiple rounds of communication within one optimization step. Under standard smoothness, strong convexity, and bounded-variance assumptions, we establish a non-asymptotic convergence guarantee that makes explicit the dependence on(µ,L,σ 2,n,R,β)and on a heterogeneity quantityG ∗ measuring the mismatch between local and global optima. The resulting bound consists of a linearly decaying transient term together with stochastic and heterogeneity-dependent residual terms. The corresponding communication-complexity consequence exhibits the scaling ˜O ( σ2 µnϵ + √ L µ 1√ 1−β ) , up to logarithmic factors, with the heterogeneity contribution entering through the residual floor in the convergence bound. This also yields the guidelineR=˜O(1/ √ 1−β) for the gossip depth. AMS subject classifications: 90C25, 68W15, 65K05 Key words: Decentralized optimization, stochastic gradient methods, distributed learning, communication complexity, gossip algorithms

Decentralized stochastic optimization has become a standard tool for large-scale learning when data and computation are distributed across many workers but a central parameter server is either undesirable or unavailable. In such systems, each node only exchanges messages with its neighbors according to an underlying communication graph. This architecture improves robustness, alleviates the single-point bottleneck of centralized synchronization, and naturally matches settings where data are generated and stored at the http://www.global-sci.org/csiam-am 1 ©20xx Global-Science Press

At the same time, local computation and network communication are tightly coupled: aggressive local updates may accelerate descent, while insufficient mixing amplifies disagreement across the network and slows global convergence. A large body of work has therefore focused on characterizing the trade-off between optimization progress and consensus error for decentralized stochastic gradient methods. Classical decentralized SGD (often called D-SGD or D-PSGD) uses one consensus step per iteration and achieves convergence guarantees that explicitly depend on the spectral gap of the mixing matrix, the condition number of the objective, and the variance of the stochastic gradients [5, 14, 17]. Subsequent methods such as EXTRA, exact diffusion, and gradient-tracking variants reduce steady-state bias and improve communication efficiency by better correcting the drift between local models and the network average [7, 11, 13, 18]. In parallel, accelerated methods and multi-consensus schemes have demonstrated that several rounds of communication per iteration, possibly combined with polynomial (Chebyshev-type) gossip, can substantially improve the dependence on the spectral gap [2, 4, 12]. Despite substantial progress on decentralized optimization, it remains useful to understand how accelerated optimization dynamics and accelerated communication primitives interact in the stochastic strongly convex regime. In particular, one would like to clarify how multiple communication rounds within each outer iteration affect the over-

Motivated by this question, we proposeMulti-Gossip Accelerated DSGD(MC-ADSGD), a decentralized stochastic optimization algorithm that combines a Nesterov-type primal– dual extrapolation with two calls to a fast gossip averaging operator (FGA) per outer iteration. The gossip depthRcontrols the number of communication rounds inside each FGA call. In the parameter regime considered in our analysis, we further couple the minibatch size and the gossip depth through the choiceB=R, so that increasingRimproves communication accuracy while also reducing gradient variance. Our focus in this paper is on presenting the proposed MC-ADSGD method and making its convergence and communication-complexity implications explicit in the strongly convex stochastic setting. Under standard smoothness, strong convexity, and boundedvariance assumptions, we derive a Lyapunov-based convergence bound consisting of a linearly decaying term together with stochastic and heterogeneity-dependent residual terms. This bound leads to a communication-complexity consequence of order ˜O ( σ2 µnϵ + √ L µ 1√ 1−β ) , up to logarithmic factors, while the heterogeneity quantityG∗ enters through the residual accuracy floor. The purpose of the present paper is therefore to give a self-contained presentation of the proposed algorithm and its analysis, and to isolate the communication-complexity consequence of the current proof in a form suitable for further comparison and extension.

blocks.text: This section briefly reviews the most relevant literature on decentralized stochastic optimization, multi-round and accelerated gossip, and communication-efficient accelerated methods, and situatesMulti-Gossip Accelerated DSGDwithin this landscape. Decentralized stochastic gradient methods.Early decentralized stochastic gradient methods such as D-SGD and D-PSGD [5, 14] apply one consensus (or gossip) step per iteration and establish convergence guarantees that explicitly depend on the spectral gap of the underlying mixing matrix. These methods are simple and widely used, but their communication complexity can be suboptimal on poorly connected graphs, and their steadystate error typically reflects a nonvanishing disagreement component. Variants based on EXTRA and exact diffusion [13, 17, 18] as well as gradient-tracking schemes such as DIGing, NEXT, and related algorithms [7, 11, 16] mitigate this issue by tracking the global gradient more accurately and correcting local drift. Many of these works operate either in deterministic or diminishing-stepsize regimes; when stochastic gradients and constant stepsizes are considered, the resulting steady-state bounds often make the dependence on noise and network parameters only partially explicit. Gradient tracking and exact diffusion.Gradient-tracking methods maintain auxiliary variables that estimate the average gradient across the network and use them to drive local updates toward the global optimum. In the deterministic setting, such methods
achieve exact convergence and, in some cases, are known to be optimal up to logarithmic
ReasFlow Paper Copilot / CSIAM Trans. Appl. Math.,x(20xx), pp. 1-25

blocks.text: factors in terms of the dependence on the condition number and the spectral gap [12]. In the stochastic strongly convex case, recent works have extended gradient tracking and exact diffusion to handle gradient noise and non-identical data distributions across nodes [10, 15]. Compared with these approaches, the proposed MC-ADSGD algorithm does not maintain an explicit gradient-tracking variable; instead, it combines a Nesterovtype primal–dual extrapolation with multi-round accelerated gossip and ties the batch size to the gossip depth. Our analysis focuses on making the communication complexity in this specific design explicit, rather than deriving a general-purpose optimality result for all gradient-tracking variants. Multi-round and accelerated gossip.The idea of performing multiple gossip rounds per iteration to accelerate consensus dates back to early work on multi-consensus methods and polynomial filtering of the mixing matrix [2, 9]. Chebyshev-accelerated gossip schemes design a polynomial in the mixing matrix that minimizes the worst-case contraction factor over the spectrum, yielding a number of rounds that scales as ˜O(1/ √ 1−β) with the inverse square root of the spectral gap. Such primitives have been used both as stand-alone averaging mechanisms [2] and as building blocks within decentralized optimization algorithms [4, 12]. The FGA operator used in the proposed MC-ADSGD method is an instance of this general idea: it implements an accelerated gossip averaging procedure with a parameterRcontrolling the number of internal communication rounds

blocks.text: and a contraction factorρthat depends explicitly onRand the spectral gap. Our contribution is to embed this primitive into a stochastic accelerated optimization algorithm and to carry out a Lyapunov analysis that tracks both the disagreement recursion and the optimization recursion. Accelerated decentralized methods and communication complexity.Beyond multiconsensus, several works have investigated acceleration in decentralized optimization, either via Nesterov-type momentum, dual acceleration, or primal–dual mirror maps [3, 4, 8, 12]. These methods often achieve communication complexity bounds that are optimal (or nearly optimal) in the deterministic strongly convex setting, with a characteristic √ L/µ/ √ 1−βdependence on the condition number and spectral gap. Extensions to time-varying or directed graphs further refine these guarantees under more general communication models [1, 6]. However, many of these results either assume exact oracles, lack fully explicit constants in the stochastic regime, or leave the relationship between the number of communication rounds per iteration and the stochastic batch size implicit. Positioning of this work.The algorithm proposed in this paper,Multi-Gossip Accelerated DSGD(MC-ADSGD), combines several ingredients that have each appeared, in different forms, in the decentralized optimization literature: local stochastic gradients, multi-round accelerated gossip, and an accelerated extrapolation structure. This section gives a concise specification of MC-ADSGD. We first state the accelerated gossip primitive used to suppress network disagreement, and then present the full iterative scheme together with its per-iteration oracle and communication costs. Communication primitive: FastGossipAverage (FGA). Main procedure: Multi-Gossip Accelerated DSGD.The iteration order is stochastic gradient→z-update (FGA)→x-update (FGA)→y-extrapolation. Design rationale and per-iteration complexity.The three state variables(x (k),z (k),y (k) ) have distinct algorithmic roles. The pointy (k) is the query location for stochastic gradients,z (k) aggregates descent information and is consensus-refined, andx(k) tracks the primal progress. We presentedMulti-Gossip Accelerated DSGD, a decentralized stochastic optimization method that combines accelerated optimization dynamics with accelerated multi-round gossip communication. The main theorem gives an explicit strongly-convex convergence guarantee with transparent dependence on the stepsize, gossip depth, spectral gap, and stochastic variance. Under the homogeneous-optimum conditionG∗ =0, the resulting communication complexity separates into a stochastic term of orderσ 2/(µnϵ)and a network term of order √ L/µ/ √ 1−β, up to logarithmic factors. From a methodological viewpoint, the analysis shows that optimization acceleration and communication acceleration should be designed together: the benefit of the extrapolation dynamics appears only when the disagreement recursion is controlled strongly enough by multi-gossip communication. This is the role of the FGA primitive and the explicit condition on ρ= √ 2(1− √ 1−β) R. A natural next step is to extend the current analysis beyond the strongly convex regime and to establish analogous explicit rates under weaker convexity assumptions. Another important direction is to understand whether a similarly explicit accelerated analysis can be carried out under more general network models, including time-varying communication patterns.

A Retraction-Free EXTRA Method for Decentralized

blocks.text: Abstract.Decentralized optimization provides a fundamental framework for largescale learning and signal processing with distributed data. We study decentralized optimization with orthogonality constraints on the Stiefel manifold and propose RF- EXTRA, a distributed retraction-free primal-dual method on static undirected networks. The method combines an approximate gradient mapping for orthogonalityconstrained optimization with an EXTRA-based decentralized recursion, thereby avoiding explicit retractions while preserving a simple communication pattern. On the theoretical side, the analysis considers both the averaged iterate and the joint error(X k−Xk,sk−sk), and establishes a contractive recursion for the joint error under an equivalent norm. This recursion is then used to compare the different terms in the descent lemma and finally derive an exactO(1/K)convergence rate for the averaged iterate under explicit parameter conditions. Experiments on PCA and low-rank matrix completion show that RF-EXTRA compares favorably with the reported decentralized baselines and exhibits strong communication efficiency on the tested tasks on the Stiefel manifold. AMS subject classifications: 65K10, 90C30, 49M37, 68W15 Key words: decentralized optimization, Stiefel manifold, retraction-free method, EXTRA, nonconvex optimization

Decentralized optimization [1, 2] studies how a network of agents cooperatively solves a global problem using local data and local communication. It has become a fundamental framework in large-scale learning [3], signal processing [4,5], and control [1], where data are naturally distributed and centralized aggregation is either costly or undesirable. In its classical Euclidean form, the goal is to combine computational scalability with communication efficiency while preserving the solution quality of the underlying centralized model. Many decentralized problems are not purely Euclidean. Such orthogonality constraints also arise in deep models with orthogonal layers [6], normalization mechanisms [7], and low-rank fine-tuning schemes [8]. Accordingly, decentralized optimization on the Stiefel manifold has become an important problem in decentralized learning and matrix optimization. A central difficulty is that decentralized primal-dual correction mechanisms and manifold feasibility mechanisms are driven by different principles. Methods in the EXTRA family are analyzed as primal-dual type recursions, whereas manifold methods typically rely on tangent projections and retractions to preserve feasibility. Once EXTRA is brought into a nonconvex problem on the Stiefel manifold, combining these two ingredients is essentially equivalent to analyzing a primal-dual algorithm together with nonconvex manifold constraints and geometry in a single recursion. The convergence analysis is hence highly nontrivial. This paper studies the consensus-constrained optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold min

Our aim is to develop a decentralized method that preserves the correction mechanism of EXTRA while using a retraction-free update on the Stiefel manifold. blocks.text: The development of decentralized optimization began with primal methods such as decentralized gradient descent (DGD) [2] and decentralized SGD type variants for stochastic objectives [10,11], which established the basic consensus optimization framework but generally suffer from steady state bias under constant stepsizes. To remove that bias, later primal-dual or correction based methods introduced auxiliary states that couple consensus and optimization more tightly. Representative milestones include gradient tracking and DGT type methods [12–14], EXTRA [4], exact diffusion [5], NIDS [15], and prox- PDA [16]. These methods clarified how exactness can be preserved over static networks while maintaining low per-iteration communication cost.

blocks.text: For orthogonality-constrained problems, decentralized Riemannian methods form the natural baseline. DRSGD [28] studies decentralized Riemannian gradient descent on the Stiefel manifold and shows that distributed PCA type tasks can be handled directly in the manifold setting. More recently, DPRGD [29] and DPRGT [30] study projected decentralized Riemannian gradient updates and decentralized proximal gradient tracking on Riemannian manifolds, respectively; together they provide our main projection based and tracking based baselines. Riemannian EXTRA (REXTRA) [31] further demonstrates that EXTRA type primal-dual correction can be extended from Euclidean space to compact submanifolds, but still through retraction or projection based updates. Related works further considered quantization and compression [32, 33], stochastic recursive momentum [34], conjugate gradient and natural gradient directions [35, 36], local linear consensus behavior on the Stiefel manifold [37], manifold consensus formulations [38,39], and decentralized retraction-free optimization on the Stiefel manifold [40]. However, an EXTRA type correction method in this retraction-free regime is still unavailable.
heading_path: Distributed optimization on the Stiefel manifold

blocks.text: A separate line of work studies orthogonality-constrained optimization without performing explicit retractions at every iteration. DESTINY [41] introduced an approximate gradient mapping for orthogonality-constrained optimization through an approximate augmented Lagrangian formulation on the Stiefel manifold, where orthogonality is controlled by a penalty-based surrogate instead of being enforced by explicit retractions at every step. Early centralized retraction-free methods also showed that one can reduce the cost of repeated QR or polar decompositions while still controlling feasibility drift [42,43]. This perspective is particularly attractive for large matrix problems, where orthogonalization can dominate the local computational budget. More recent developments include infeasible methods with local linear convergence guarantees [44], ambient-space reformulations that dissolve hard constraints into smooth penalty structures [45], and preconditioned schemes motivated by LoRA type largemodel fine-tuning [8]. Related applications in orthogonal weight normalization and multi-Stiefel learning further illustrate the practical importance of low-cost updates for orthogonality-constrained problems [6, 7]. The present work draws on this line to construct the local geometric step, and it combines that step with the decentralized EXTRA correction mechanism discussed above.

blocks.text: This paper combines decentralized primal-dual correction, distributed optimization on the Stiefel manifold, and retraction-free orthogonality control in a single scheme. The key idea is to embed an approximate gradient mapping for orthogonality-constrained optimization into an EXTRA recursion. Our contributions are summarized as follows. • We design and implement RF-EXTRA, a distributed retraction-free EXTRA algorithm that combines an approximate gradient mapping for orthogonalityconstrained optimization with an EXTRA-based decentralized recursion on the Stiefel manifold, and we validate this design through a systematic numerical study on PCA and LRMC over the Stiefel manifold. • On the theory side, we show that the joint-error variables(X k−Xk,sk−sk)remain in a controllable region and satisfy a contractive recursion under an equivalent norm. This allows us to establish a summed joint-error bound, compare the different terms in the descent analysis of the original objective function, and finally derive an exactO(1/K)convergence rate under a constant stepsize. In contrast to existing retraction-based EXTRA-type methods such as REXTRA [31] and existing retraction-free schemes without EXTRA correction, our analysis must couple retraction-free feasibility control with an EXTRA-type inexact primal-dual recursion; this combination is nontrivial because of the manifold nonconvexity, especially under a constant stepsize, as also noted in [31]. LetW∈R n×n be a symmetric doubly stochastic mixing matrix associated with a connected undirected graph, and let V=θI n +(1−θ)W,θ∈(0,1/2]. We use the lifted mixing matricesWandVintroduced in the notation section. Our construction starts from the Euclidean correction philosophy of EXTRA and then replaces the Euclidean gradient with a surrogate compatible with the geometry of the Stiefel manifold. For unconstrained consensus optimization, EXTRA corrects the steady state bias of decentralized gradient descent by coupling the primal recursion with a memory term. To this end, we replace the Euclidean gradient by an approximate gradient mapping for orthogonality-constrained optimization [41]. This construction allows the geometric information to enter through a local mapH i without changing the linear communication structure of EXTRA. For the averaged analysis, we also use the corresponding global map H(X) =G(X)+βX(X ⊤X−I r), whereGis defined fromf:=n −1 ∑n i=1 fi in the same way asG i is defined fromf i. After introducing the algorithm, we write Hk := [H1(X1,k)⊤,...,H n(Xn,k)⊤]⊤, ¯Hk := 1 n n ∑ i=1 Hi(Xi,k). The resulting algorithm, called RF-EXTRA, is stated in Algorithm 1. The initialization follows the EXTRA mechanism and uses the local mapH i evaluated at the initial point. In stacked form, Algorithm 1 reads Xk+1 =WX k +s k, (2.3) sk+1 =s k +(W−V)X k−α(H k+1−H k). (2.4) Averaging (2.3)–(2.4) and using the doubly stochasticity ofWandVyields ¯sk =−α ¯Hk, ¯Xk+1 = ¯Xk−α ¯Hk. This averaged recursion is the key link between RF-EXTRA and the descent analysis developed in Section 3. RF-EXTRA has two main advantages. First, it preserves the EXTRA mechanism, so the communication layer remains linear and fully decentralized. Second, it avoids explicit retractions at every iteration. Each step requires one neighbor mixing update forXk, one evaluation of the local surrogate mapH i, and one auxiliary correction update fors k. Consequently, the method replaces repeated orthogonalization with a cheaper ambientspace computation while still maintaining effective control of feasibility and consensus
through the penalty term and the correction state.

We proposed RF-EXTRA, a decentralized retraction-free method for optimization on the Stiefel manifold. The method combines an ambient-space surrogate for the orthogonality-constrained local models with an EXTRA-based primal-dual recursion, thereby preserving a simple decentralized communication structure while avoiding explicit per-iteration retractions. On the theoretical side, the analysis is built on the averaged iterate and the joint error (Xk−Xk,sk−sk). By establishing a contractive recursion for the joint error under an equivalent norm and then comparing the different terms in the descent analysis, we obtain an exactO(1/K)convergence guarantee for the averaged iterate. The experiments indicate that RF-EXTRA is a competitive retraction-free decentralized solver for optimization problems on the Stiefel manifold. On PCA and low-rank matrix completion, it delivers favorable empirical performance and communication efficiency relative to the reported baselines. These results support retraction-free decen-
